questions.prompt: Give four features of a valid comparison of amylase activity at different pH values.
scheme: 1 · Use buffers to maintain each pH.
2 · Maintain the same temperature using a water bath.
3 · Use the same initial enzyme and substrate concentrations and volumes.
4 · Repeat independently and compare a consistent initial-rate measure.

questions.prompt: Why randomly allocate seedlings to treatments?
scheme: Random allocation distributes pre-existing differences without systematic treatment bias.

questions.prompt: Which samples biological variation?
options: Sampling leaves from three independent plants
scheme: Independent plants provide biological replicates.

questions.prompt: Explain the benefits of a colorimeter blank and independent repeats.
scheme: 1 · A blank corrects the baseline contribution of the solvent and container.
2 · Independent repeats reveal variation in the procedure or organisms.
3 · Repeats allow calculation of a mean and a measure of spread.

questions.prompt: A mass change is 2.0 g with uncertainty 0.1 g. Calculate percentage uncertainty.
A line rises from 2 to 8 cm³ in 3 minutes. Calculate the gradient.

descriptive-statistics.title: Means, standard deviation and standard error

questions.prompt: Two samples have equal means but SD values of 2 mm and 8 mm. Interpret this and explain why sample size is needed.
scheme: 1 · The sample with SD 8 mm has more spread among individual observations.
2 · Equal means do not imply equal distributions.
3 · Sample size is needed to calculate SE or carry out an appropriate inferential test.

questions.prompt: SD is 6 mm and n = 9. Calculate SE.
If n rises fourfold while SD is unchanged, SE usually…
scheme: The square root of n doubles.

statistical-tests.title: t tests, chi-squared and Spearman rank

questions.prompt: A suitable t test gives p = 0.02 at a prespecified 5% significance level. Interpret the evidence.
scheme: 1 · Reject the null hypothesis of no population mean difference at the 5% level.
2 · The result provides evidence of a population mean difference under the test assumptions.
3 · It does not by itself establish causation or remove confounding.

questions.prompt: Which test compares offspring counts with a predicted 3:1 ratio?
scheme: These are categorical frequencies compared with expected counts.

questions.prompt: Observed counts are 30 and 10; expected counts are 20 and 20. Calculate χ².

practical-endorsement.title: PAGs, research and the Practical Endorsement

questions.prompt: Explain a benefit and two limitations of using only a computer model to infer a population trend.
scheme: 1 · A model allows assumptions and variables to be explored systematically.
2 · Predictions depend on the assumptions and parameters selected.
3 · Independent field data are needed to test whether predictions describe the real population.

questions.prompt: Which alone awards the Practical Endorsement?
scheme: The centre assesses demonstrated practical competence.

questions.prompt: Why record author, source URL and access date?
scheme: References allow readers to inspect the evidence.

questions.prompt: A 5 µm scale bar measures 20 mm. A chloroplast in the same image measures 32 mm. Calculate its actual length.
scheme: 1 · Use the ratio 32 / 20 × 5.
2 · The actual length is 8 µm.

questions.prompt: A 50 µm cell appears 20 mm long. Calculate magnification.
Which best reveals mitochondrial cristae?
scheme: TEM resolves internal membranes in a thin section.

questions.prompt: Explain three adaptations of a cell secreting many protein enzymes.
scheme: 1 · Extensive rough ER and ribosomes synthesise protein.
2 · A large Golgi apparatus modifies and packages enzymes into vesicles.
3 · Many mitochondria provide ATP for synthesis and transport.

questions.prompt: Which modifies and sorts secreted proteins?
scheme: The Golgi receives and processes proteins from the ER.

questions.prompt: Which distinguishes bacterial from animal cytosol?
scheme: Both cell types contain DNA and a membrane.

questions.prompt: Explain why glycogen is a suitable carbohydrate store.
scheme: 1 · It is relatively insoluble and has little osmotic effect compared with free glucose.
2 · Its compact polymer structure stores many glucose residues.
3 · Many branch ends allow rapid hydrolysis and glucose release.

questions.prompt: Cellulose is made from…
scheme: β-glucose forms straight β-1,4-linked chains.

questions.prompt: Why neutralise after acid hydrolysis before Benedict’s testing?
scheme: Residual acid interferes with the alkaline test.

questions.prompt: Explain why phospholipids form a bilayer in water.
scheme: 1 · Hydrophilic heads interact with water.
2 · Hydrophobic tails face away from water.
3 · Two layers arrange with tails inward and heads facing aqueous fluid on both sides.

questions.prompt: Which bonds link glycerol and fatty acids?
scheme: Three ester bonds form in a triglyceride.

questions.prompt: Which water property limits rapid temperature change?
scheme: A large energy transfer is required for a given temperature change.

questions.prompt: Explain why replacing one amino acid can alter enzyme activity.
scheme: 1 · The replacement changes possible R-group interactions.
2 · This can alter tertiary folding and the active site.
3 · Substrate binding or catalysis may become less effective.

questions.prompt: Which bond joins amino acid residues?
scheme: A peptide bond forms between amino and carboxyl groups.

questions.prompt: Which level describes amino acid order?
scheme: Primary structure is the sequence.

questions.prompt: Describe how to compare amylase initial rates at different substrate concentrations.
scheme: 1 · Keep enzyme concentration, pH and temperature constant.
2 · Measure a product or substrate signal frequently after mixing.
3 · Plot signal against time and calculate initial tangent gradients.
4 · Repeat independently and compare mean rates and spread.

questions.prompt: Why does rate plateau as substrate rises?
scheme: Active sites are occupied most of the time.

questions.prompt: Extra substrate can reduce which effect in a simple model?
scheme: Substrate and inhibitor compete for the same site.

questions.prompt: Explain how DNA structure permits accurate copying.
scheme: 1 · Strands separate when hydrogen bonds between bases are disrupted.
2 · Each original strand supplies a template.
3 · Complementary base pairing determines the new strand sequence.

questions.prompt: Which DNA base pairs with guanine?
scheme: G pairs with C.

questions.prompt: Double-stranded DNA contains 30% adenine. What percentage is guanine?
scheme: T is 30%; C plus G is 40%, so G is 20%.

questions.prompt: Explain why a base substitution can leave the polypeptide unchanged.
scheme: 1 · The code is degenerate.
2 · The changed codon may specify the same amino acid.

questions.prompt: Template DNA TAC gives which mRNA codon?
scheme: RNA uses U rather than T.

questions.prompt: Which bonds form during translation?
scheme: Ribosomes catalyse peptide bond formation.

questions.prompt: Explain why high temperature increases beetroot pigment leakage.
scheme: 1 · Molecular motion and membrane fluidity increase.
2 · At sufficiently high temperature membrane proteins and bilayer organisation are disrupted.
3 · Greater permeability permits more pigment to leave cells.

questions.prompt: Movement of ions against a gradient requires…
scheme: Transport against an electrochemical gradient requires energy.

questions.prompt: Water enters when external water potential is…
scheme: Net movement is from higher to lower water potential.

cell-cycle.title: Cell cycle, mitosis and stem cells

questions.prompt: Explain why mitotic daughter nuclei normally contain the same genetic information.
scheme: 1 · Replication forms identical sister chromatids before division.
2 · The spindle separates sister chromatids into opposite nuclei.
3 · Each daughter receives one copy of every chromosome.

questions.prompt: 24 of 120 cells are in mitosis. Calculate mitotic index. Give the mitotic index as a decimal.
When do sister chromatids separate?
scheme: Anaphase moves chromatids to opposite poles.

questions.prompt: Explain two meiotic sources of variation.
scheme: 1 · Crossing over exchanges DNA between non-sister chromatids of homologues.
2 · This forms new combinations of alleles along a chromosome.
3 · Independent orientation and segregation produces different combinations of maternal and paternal homologues.

questions.prompt: What separates in anaphase I?
scheme: Sister chromatids remain together in division I.

questions.prompt: A diploid organism has 16 chromosomes. How many are in a normal gamete?
scheme: Meiosis halves the number.

questions.prompt: Explain three adaptations of alveoli for rapid oxygen uptake.
scheme: 1 · Many alveoli provide a large total surface area.
2 · Thin alveolar epithelium and capillary endothelium reduce diffusion distance.
3 · Ventilation and blood flow maintain a steep oxygen concentration gradient.

questions.prompt: Which change increases diffusion rate?
scheme: A larger area allows more particles to cross per unit time.

questions.prompt: Why is countercurrent flow efficient?
options: It maintains an oxygen gradient along the lamella
scheme: Blood meets water of higher oxygen concentration along the surface.

questions.prompt: A trace shows 12 breaths in 30 s, each 0.5 dm³. Calculate minute ventilation.
scheme: 1 · Breathing frequency = 24 breaths per minute.
2 · Minute ventilation = 24 × 0.5 = 12 dm³ min⁻¹.

questions.prompt: Tidal volume is 0.6 dm³ and frequency is 15 min⁻¹. Calculate minute ventilation.
Which volume remains after maximum expiration?
scheme: Residual volume remains in the lungs.

heart.title: Heart structure and the cardiac cycle

questions.prompt: Explain how excitation normally produces coordinated ventricular contraction.
scheme: 1 · The AV node delays excitation after atrial excitation.
2 · The bundle of His conducts excitation towards the apex.
3 · Purkyne tissue distributes excitation so contraction moves upwards from the apex.

questions.prompt: Heart rate is 75 min⁻¹ and stroke volume 70 cm³. Calculate cardiac output in dm³ min⁻¹.
scheme: 75 × 70 = 5250 cm³ min⁻¹ = 5.25 dm³ min⁻¹.

questions.prompt: What prevents backflow into the left atrium?
scheme: The left atrioventricular valve closes when ventricular pressure rises.

blood-tissue-fluid.title: Blood vessels, tissue fluid and lymph

questions.prompt: Explain how loss of plasma proteins can promote tissue swelling.
scheme: 1 · Reduced plasma protein concentration lowers the inward oncotic effect.
2 · More fluid remains in or enters the tissue spaces relative to its removal.
3 · Fluid accumulation can exceed lymphatic return and cause swelling.

questions.prompt: Which vessel provides the main thin exchange barrier?
scheme: Capillary endothelium is thin and close to tissues.

questions.prompt: What returns excess tissue fluid?
scheme: Lymphatics return fluid and proteins to the circulation.

questions.prompt: Explain the benefit of the Bohr effect in exercising muscle.
scheme: 1 · Respiration produces more carbon dioxide and associated acidity.
2 · Haemoglobin oxygen affinity decreases and the curve shifts right.
3 · More oxygen unloads at the tissue partial pressure to support aerobic respiration.

questions.prompt: At the same oxygen partial pressure, a right-shifted curve means…
scheme: A right shift indicates lower oxygen affinity.

questions.prompt: Fetal haemoglobin normally has…
options: Higher oxygen affinity than adult haemoglobin
scheme: Its higher affinity supports placental oxygen transfer.

questions.prompt: Explain why increasing air movement can increase transpiration.
scheme: 1 · Air movement removes humid air around the leaf.
2 · The water-vapour concentration gradient from the leaf to the air becomes steeper.
3 · Water vapour diffuses away more rapidly if stomata remain sufficiently open.

questions.prompt: What bonds support cohesion between water molecules?
scheme: Hydrogen bonding creates cohesion.

questions.prompt: A potometer directly measures…
scheme: Uptake is used as an approximation to water loss.

questions.prompt: Explain how loading sucrose at a source initiates pressure flow.
scheme: 1 · Sucrose loading lowers sieve-tube water potential.
2 · Water enters by osmosis from surrounding tissue or xylem.
3 · Hydrostatic pressure rises and drives flow towards lower-pressure sinks.

questions.prompt: A growing root receiving sucrose is a…
scheme: It imports assimilates for growth and respiration.

questions.prompt: What drives bulk flow through a sieve tube?
scheme: Loading and unloading establish pressure differences.

questions.prompt: Explain how mucus and cilia reduce respiratory infection risk.
scheme: 1 · Mucus traps particles and pathogens.
2 · Cilia move the mucus towards the throat.
3 · Removal and swallowing reduce the number of pathogens reaching deeper gas-exchange surfaces.

questions.prompt: Which is a protoctist pathogen?
scheme: Plasmodium is transmitted by mosquito vectors.

questions.prompt: What normally follows phagosome formation?
options: Immediate antibody secretion by the phagocyte
scheme: Lysosomal enzymes digest enclosed material.

questions.prompt: Describe how a specific B-cell response develops after antigen exposure.
scheme: 1 · A B cell with a complementary receptor recognises the antigen and receives activation signals.
2 · The selected cell divides by clonal expansion.
3 · Some descendants become plasma cells secreting specific antibody.
4 · Others become memory cells for future responses.

questions.prompt: Which cells secrete large quantities of antibodies?
scheme: Plasma cells are differentiated B-cell descendants.

questions.prompt: Why is a secondary response faster?
options: The pathogen becomes harmless in every case
scheme: Memory populations rapidly expand on re-exposure.

questions.prompt: Explain how an antibiotic-resistant bacterial population can become common during treatment.
scheme: 1 · Resistance already exists through mutation or acquired genes in some bacteria.
2 · The antibiotic kills or inhibits susceptible bacteria more strongly.
3 · Resistant survivors reproduce and pass on resistance, increasing its frequency.

questions.prompt: Which normally gives immediate temporary protection without generating memory?
scheme: Transferred antibodies act immediately but are later broken down.

questions.prompt: Why do antibiotics not directly treat influenza virus?
scheme: Virus replication relies on host machinery rather than bacterial structures.

questions.prompt: Explain three requirements for a valid mark–recapture estimate.
scheme: 1 · Marked organisms mix with the population before resampling.
2 · Marks remain identifiable and do not alter survival or capture probability.
3 · Births, deaths, immigration and emigration are negligible over the sampling period.

questions.prompt: 20 animals are marked. A second sample contains 30 animals, six marked. Estimate population size.
Two sites have equal richness. Which can still differ?
options: The number of species by definition
scheme: The species can have very different relative abundances.

questions.prompt: Explain why similar body shapes in unrelated aquatic animals do not necessarily indicate a recent common ancestor.
scheme: 1 · Similar environments impose similar selection pressures.
2 · Different lineages can evolve similar functional adaptations independently.
3 · This is convergent evolution, so additional homologous or molecular evidence is required.

questions.prompt: Which pair forms a binomial name?
scheme: The binomial combines genus and species.

questions.prompt: Why can DNA evidence revise classification?
options: It provides evidence of relatedness not obvious from appearance
It makes fossils unnecessary in every study
scheme: Molecular comparisons can reveal previously hidden evolutionary relationships.

questions.prompt: Explain how pesticide resistance can increase in an insect population.
scheme: 1 · Heritable variation means some insects carry resistance alleles.
2 · Pesticide exposure kills susceptible insects more readily.
3 · Resistant insects leave more offspring that inherit resistance.
4 · Resistance alleles increase in frequency across generations.

questions.prompt: Which creates new alleles?
scheme: Meiosis and fertilisation rearrange existing alleles.

questions.prompt: Chance allele-frequency change is…
scheme: Drift is especially strong in small populations.

questions.prompt: Explain how negative feedback stabilises a regulated variable.
scheme: 1 · A receptor detects a deviation from the regulated range.
2 · A coordination system activates an appropriate effector.
3 · The effector response reduces the deviation and feedback reduces stimulation.

questions.prompt: Negative feedback usually…
scheme: The response acts to bring the regulated variable back towards its range.

questions.prompt: Why do only some cells respond to a circulating hormone?
scheme: Receptor complementarity determines response.

questions.prompt: Explain why excess amino acids increase urea production.
scheme: 1 · Excess amino acids are deaminated.
2 · Their amino groups produce toxic ammonia.
3 · The liver converts ammonia to less toxic urea for excretion.

questions.prompt: Where is most urea synthesised?
scheme: The liver converts ammonia into urea.

questions.prompt: Which is egestion?
scheme: Undigested gut contents are egested.

questions.prompt: Explain three proximal-tubule adaptations for reabsorption.
scheme: 1 · Microvilli increase the membrane surface area.
2 · Many mitochondria supply ATP for ion pumping.
3 · Carrier proteins enable selective transport, including sodium-linked glucose uptake.

questions.prompt: Which is normally largely retained in glomerular blood?
scheme: The filtration barrier restricts large proteins and cells.

questions.prompt: What supports glucose cotransport in the PCT?
scheme: A sodium gradient maintained by active transport supplies the driving force.

questions.prompt: Describe the response to a fall in blood water potential.
scheme: 1 · Hypothalamic osmoreceptors detect the change.
2 · More ADH is released from the posterior pituitary.
3 · More aquaporins increase collecting-duct water permeability.
4 · More water is reabsorbed by osmosis and urine becomes more concentrated.

questions.prompt: More ADH usually produces…
scheme: More water is reabsorbed from collecting ducts.

questions.prompt: Why include glucose at an appropriate concentration in dialysis fluid?
options: To limit net glucose loss from blood
scheme: An appropriate concentration reduces an unwanted glucose gradient.

questions.prompt: Explain how myelination increases conduction speed.
scheme: 1 · Myelin electrically insulates sections of axon.
2 · Action potentials regenerate mainly at nodes of Ranvier.
3 · Local currents spread between nodes so saltatory conduction is faster than continuous regeneration.

questions.prompt: What causes the rapid depolarising upstroke?
options: The cell losing all ATP instantly
scheme: Sodium channels open above threshold and sodium enters down its electrochemical gradient.

questions.prompt: Stronger stimulation commonly increases…
scheme: Frequency codes intensity while amplitude remains approximately fixed.

questions.prompt: Describe transmission across a cholinergic chemical synapse.
scheme: 1 · An arriving impulse opens calcium channels and calcium enters.
2 · Vesicles release acetylcholine by exocytosis.
3 · Acetylcholine diffuses across the cleft and binds postsynaptic receptors.
4 · Receptor activation changes ion permeability and can initiate a postsynaptic impulse if threshold is reached.

questions.prompt: Which ion triggers vesicle release?
scheme: Calcium entry initiates vesicle fusion.

questions.prompt: Several inputs at different synapses combine. This is…
scheme: Spatial summation integrates inputs from different locations.

questions.prompt: Explain how glucagon helps correct low blood glucose.
scheme: 1 · Low glucose stimulates pancreatic α cells to release glucagon.
2 · Glucagon binds receptors on liver cells and activates signalling.
3 · Glycogen breakdown and glucose synthesis increase glucose release.
4 · Rising blood glucose reduces the original stimulus through negative feedback.

questions.prompt: Which pancreatic cells secrete insulin?
scheme: β cells respond to raised glucose.

questions.prompt: Glycogenolysis means…
scheme: It releases glucose units from glycogen.

questions.prompt: Explain how calcium and ATP enable skeletal muscle contraction.
scheme: 1 · Calcium binds troponin and moves tropomyosin to expose actin binding sites.
2 · Myosin binds actin and performs a power stroke.
3 · ATP binding detaches myosin and ATP hydrolysis re-energises the head for further cycling.

questions.prompt: What binds calcium during skeletal-muscle activation?
scheme: Troponin changes shape and shifts tropomyosin.

questions.prompt: Movement directed towards a stimulus is…
scheme: Taxis is a directional response.

questions.prompt: Plan three controls when testing auxin concentration on root growth.
scheme: 1 · Use seedlings of the same species and comparable initial age and size.
2 · Keep light, temperature, water and exposure duration constant.
3 · Include a solvent-only or zero-auxin control and independent replicate seedlings.

questions.prompt: Which hormone is strongly associated with seed germination and reserve mobilisation?
scheme: Gibberellin promotes enzyme production during germination.

questions.prompt: A shoot bends towards light because…
options: Cells on its sides elongate unequally
scheme: Differential elongation creates curvature.

questions.prompt: Explain how light-dependent reactions produce ATP.
scheme: 1 · Light-excited electron transport supports proton accumulation inside thylakoids.
2 · This establishes an electrochemical proton gradient.
3 · Protons return through ATP synthase, driving ATP formation from ADP and phosphate.

questions.prompt: The oxygen released in photosynthesis originates from…
scheme: Photolysis of water releases oxygen.

questions.prompt: A pigment travels 36 mm and the solvent front 60 mm. Calculate Rf.

calvin-cycle.title: The Calvin cycle and limiting factors

questions.prompt: Explain why low carbon dioxide supply can reduce carbohydrate synthesis despite bright light.
scheme: 1 · Less carbon dioxide is available for Rubisco-catalysed fixation.
2 · Less GP is formed and therefore less TP can be produced.
3 · Carbon assimilation limits carbohydrate production even if ATP and reduced NADP are available.

questions.prompt: Where does the Calvin cycle occur?
scheme: Carbon fixation occurs in chloroplast stroma.

questions.prompt: At the compensation point…
options: Photosynthesis and respiration balance in net gas exchange
scheme: Equal opposing rates give zero net exchange.

glycolysis.title: Respiration: glycolysis and the link reaction

questions.prompt: Summarise the link reaction for one pyruvate molecule.
scheme: 1 · One carbon dioxide is removed by decarboxylation.
2 · NAD is reduced during oxidation.
3 · The two-carbon acetate combines with coenzyme A to form acetyl-CoA.

questions.prompt: How many pyruvate molecules arise from one glucose?
scheme: A six-carbon glucose yields two three-carbon pyruvates.

questions.prompt: Which is released in the link reaction?
scheme: Pyruvate is decarboxylated before acetyl-CoA forms.

questions.prompt: Explain why oxygen deprivation reduces ATP production in mitochondria.
scheme: 1 · Oxygen can no longer accept electrons at the end of the electron-transport chain.
2 · Electron flow and associated proton pumping stop.
3 · The proton gradient can no longer be sustained for ATP synthase.
4 · Reduced coenzymes cannot be reoxidised normally, restricting upstream aerobic pathways.

questions.prompt: The final electron acceptor in aerobic respiration is…
scheme: Oxygen accepts electrons and protons to form water.

questions.prompt: How many carbon dioxide molecules are released by two Krebs-cycle turns?
scheme: Each acetyl-CoA gives two carbon dioxide.

questions.prompt: Explain three controls in a respirometer comparison at different temperatures.
scheme: 1 · Allow apparatus and organisms to equilibrate at each temperature.
2 · Use a suitable control to correct for non-metabolic gas-volume changes.
3 · Standardise organism mass and time interval, and ensure sufficient oxygen supply.

questions.prompt: An organism produces 8 cm³ CO₂ while consuming 10 cm³ O₂. Calculate RQ.
Why regenerate NAD without oxygen?
scheme: Glycolysis needs oxidised NAD as an electron acceptor.

questions.prompt: Explain why a one-base deletion near the start of a coding region may have a greater effect than a substitution.
scheme: 1 · The deletion can shift the reading frame.
2 · Many downstream codons can change and a premature stop may occur.
3 · A substitution usually affects only one codon and may be silent.

questions.prompt: Deleting one coding base can cause…
options: A new chromosome in every case
scheme: Downstream codon grouping changes.

questions.prompt: A silent substitution…
options: Can leave the amino acid unchanged
scheme: Different codons can encode the same amino acid.

gene-regulation.title: Gene regulation, lac operon and development

questions.prompt: Explain induction of lac structural-gene expression when a suitable inducer is present.
scheme: 1 · The inducer binds to the repressor and changes its conformation.
2 · The repressor no longer binds the operator effectively.
3 · RNA polymerase can transcribe the structural genes under otherwise suitable conditions.

questions.prompt: In the basic lac model, the repressor binds the…
scheme: Operator binding inhibits transcription.

questions.prompt: DNA methylation changes…
options: Gene regulation without necessarily changing base sequence
scheme: Epigenetic marks influence expression.

questions.prompt: For Aa × aa, predict genotypes and phenotypes under complete dominance.
scheme: 1 · The first parent produces A and a gametes; the second produces a gametes.
2 · Expected genotypes are 1 Aa : 1 aa.
3 · Expected phenotypes are 1 dominant : 1 recessive.

questions.prompt: In Aa × Aa with complete dominance, what fraction are aa?
scheme: One of four equally likely combinations is aa.

questions.prompt: A codominant heterozygote…
scheme: Both allelic contributions are detectable.

questions.prompt: Explain why two genes on the same chromosome may not produce equal gamete frequencies.
scheme: 1 · They are linked and tend to pass into the same gamete together.
2 · Crossing over can create recombinant allele combinations.
3 · If crossing over between the loci is limited, parental combinations are more frequent.

questions.prompt: An excess of parental types in a test cross can indicate…
options: A guaranteed mutation in every gamete
scheme: Linked alleles tend to remain together unless recombination occurs.

questions.prompt: There are 40 recombinants among 200 offspring. Calculate recombination percentage.
A small founder population has different allele frequencies from its source. Explain a mechanism without assuming selection.
scheme: 1 · The founders are a small non-representative sample of the original gene pool.
2 · Chance sampling changes allele frequencies.
3 · This founder effect is a form of genetic drift.

questions.prompt: The recessive phenotype frequency is 0.09 under Hardy–Weinberg. Calculate q.
If p = 0.7 and q = 0.3, calculate heterozygote frequency.
Explain the three main stages of a PCR cycle.
scheme: 1 · Heating separates complementary DNA strands.
2 · Cooling allows primers to anneal to target sequences.
3 · Thermostable polymerase extends primers using free nucleotides.

questions.prompt: Starting with one target molecule, ideal doubling occurs for five cycles. How many copies result?
Which DNA fragments usually travel farther in the same gel run?
scheme: Smaller fragments move through the matrix more readily.

questions.prompt: Explain three features needed to express a human protein gene in a bacterial host.
scheme: 1 · A suitable coding sequence, often cDNA without introns.
2 · A vector with bacterial replication and appropriate promoter features.
3 · A method to introduce the vector and identify transformed cells with the desired construct.

questions.prompt: Which enzyme joins DNA fragments?
scheme: Ligase forms phosphodiester bonds.

questions.prompt: Why use cDNA for bacterial expression of some human genes?
options: It lacks introns removed from mature mRNA
It automatically includes every bacterial promoter
scheme: Bacteria generally cannot splice eukaryotic introns as human cells do.

questions.prompt: Describe three stages of micropropagation after choosing a suitable parent plant.
scheme: 1 · Take and surface-sterilise an explant using an approved protocol.
2 · Culture aseptically on suitable nutrient and hormone media to generate shoots and roots.
3 · Acclimatise plantlets before transfer to soil.

questions.prompt: What is an explant?
options: A piece of plant tissue used to start culture
scheme: An explant provides starting tissue for plant culture.

questions.prompt: A major risk of genetic uniformity is…
scheme: A pathogen able to infect one genotype may affect the whole crop.

questions.prompt: Explain why a nuclear-transfer clone may not be identical in every respect to the nucleus donor.
scheme: 1 · Mitochondrial DNA comes mainly from the egg donor.
2 · Developmental environment can affect phenotype.
3 · Epigenetic reprogramming and new mutations can alter gene expression or sequence.

questions.prompt: In nuclear transfer, the egg nucleus is…
scheme: Enucleation avoids retaining the egg’s nuclear genome.

questions.prompt: Most mitochondrial DNA in a nuclear-transfer clone derives from…
scheme: Mitochondria are present in the egg cytoplasm.

questions.prompt: Explain four controls needed in an aerobic industrial microbial culture.
scheme: 1 · Control temperature to maintain enzyme activity without damaging cells.
2 · Control pH to maintain suitable cellular enzyme conditions.
3 · Supply oxygen and mix to support aerobic respiration throughout the culture.
4 · Maintain aseptic conditions to prevent contamination and loss of product purity.

questions.prompt: During stationary phase, population size is roughly stable because…
options: Cell production and loss are approximately balanced
scheme: Resource limitation and waste accumulation affect net growth.

questions.prompt: A benefit of immobilising lactase is…
scheme: The enzyme remains associated with its support.

questions.prompt: Explain the role of microorganisms in returning nitrogen from dead organisms to the atmosphere.
scheme: 1 · Decomposers release ammonium through ammonification.
2 · Nitrifying microorganisms convert ammonium through nitrite to nitrate.
3 · Denitrifying microorganisms convert nitrate to nitrogen gas under suitable conditions.

questions.prompt: Which process converts nitrate to nitrogen gas?
scheme: Denitrification returns nitrogen to the atmosphere.

questions.prompt: Which normally begins after disturbance with soil remaining?
scheme: Soil and biological legacies distinguish secondary succession.

questions.prompt: Explain three reasons why not all producer production becomes herbivore production.
scheme: 1 · Not all producer material is eaten.
2 · Some eaten material is not assimilated and is egested.
3 · Assimilated energy supports respiration and is dissipated, leaving less for growth.

questions.prompt: GPP is 2400 and producer respiration is 900 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹. Calculate NPP.
Consumers receive 180 from 1500 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹ of producer NPP. Calculate transfer efficiency.
Explain why a fishing quota should be reviewed regularly.
scheme: 1 · Birth, growth, death and recruitment rates can change.
2 · Environmental conditions and food-web interactions alter population recovery.
3 · Updated monitoring is needed to keep harvest below a level that depletes the stock.

questions.prompt: A population starts at 200, with 35 births, 20 deaths, 10 immigrants and 5 emigrants. Find the final size.
Competition between members of the same species is…
scheme: Intraspecific competition occurs within a species.

questions.prompt: Evaluate habitat corridors using two potential benefits and one limitation.
scheme: 1 · They can allow movement between isolated populations.
2 · This can support gene flow and recolonisation.
3 · They can also facilitate spread of pathogens or invasive species, so monitoring and context matter.

questions.prompt: Which is an ex-situ strategy?
scheme: Seeds are stored outside their natural habitat.

questions.prompt: Why manage relatedness in captive breeding?
options: To limit inbreeding and retain diversity
To ensure every offspring is genetically identical
scheme: Genetic management reduces inbreeding and diversity loss.

questions.prompt: Section A · Multiple choice 1Select one answer. Which organelle normally modifies proteins received from rough ER?
scheme: 1 · B: Golgi apparatus.

questions.prompt: Section A · Multiple choice 2Select one answer. Which cell component is found in a typical bacterium?
scheme: 1 · C: 70S ribosomes.

questions.prompt: Section A · Multiple choice 3Select one answer. A cell image is 12 mm wide and the cell is 30 µm wide. What is magnification?
Section A · Multiple choice 4Select one answer. Which reaction forms a peptide bond?
scheme: 1 · A: Condensation between amino acids.

questions.prompt: Section A · Multiple choice 5Select one answer. Which feature distinguishes cellulose from amylose?
scheme: 1 · A: It contains β-glucose.

questions.prompt: Section A · Multiple choice 6Select one answer. Which change directly raises facilitated diffusion rate before carrier saturation?
scheme: 1 · A: A steeper substrate gradient.

questions.prompt: Section A · Multiple choice 7Select one answer. Which enzyme adds complementary DNA nucleotides during replication?
scheme: 1 · B: DNA polymerase.

questions.prompt: Section A · Multiple choice 8Select one answer. What separates in mitotic anaphase?
scheme: 1 · B: Sister chromatids.

questions.prompt: Section A · Multiple choice 9Select one answer. Which factor shifts an adult haemoglobin dissociation curve to the right?
scheme: 1 · A: Higher carbon dioxide concentration.

questions.prompt: Section A · Multiple choice 10Select one answer. Which event initiates the normal cardiac electrical cycle?
scheme: 1 · B: SAN excitation.

questions.prompt: Section A · Multiple choice 11Select one answer. Which process does a shoot potometer directly estimate?
scheme: 1 · A: Water uptake.

questions.prompt: Section A · Multiple choice 12Select one answer. Where is most urea produced?
scheme: 1 · C: Liver.

questions.prompt: Section A · Multiple choice 13Select one answer. Which event depolarises an axon during the action-potential upstroke?
scheme: 1 · A: Sodium entry.

questions.prompt: Section A · Multiple choice 14Select one answer. What is the final electron acceptor in aerobic respiration?
scheme: 1 · B: Oxygen.

questions.prompt: Section A · Multiple choice 15Select one answer. Which process produces ATP without reduced NADP or oxygen in a chloroplast?
scheme: 1 · A: Cyclic photophosphorylation.

questions.prompt: A secretory cell and an enzyme investigationA student studies enzyme-secreting cells. A cell measures 28 graticule divisions; calibration shows 10 divisions represent 15 µm. An enzyme from the cells is tested at substrate concentrations of 1, 2, 4 and 8 mmol dm⁻³. scheme: 1 · One division represents 15/10 = 1.5 µm.

questions.prompt: Replication and dividing root cellsA root-tip sample contains 240 cells, including 36 in mitosis. The organism has a diploid chromosome number of 12. A template DNA segment is TAC GGA TTT. Compare mitosis with meiosis for this organism.

3 · Mitosis involves one nuclear division whereas meiosis involves two after one replication.
4 · Meiosis includes homologous pairing and crossing over that contribute to variation.

questions.prompt: Water and assimilate transport in a plantA potometer capillary has cross-sectional area 0.40 mm². A bubble moves 60 mm in 5 minutes. questions.prompt: Kidney regulation during dehydrationAfter prolonged exercise without drinking, an individual has a lower blood water potential and a smaller volume of more concentrated urine. 4 · More water returns to blood by osmosis down the medullary gradient, producing a smaller volume of more concentrated urine.

questions.prompt: Kidney regulation during dehydrationAfter prolonged exercise without drinking, an individual has a lower blood water potential and a smaller volume of more concentrated urine. scheme: 1 · Excess amino acids are deaminated in the liver.

4 · Urea travels in blood to kidneys and is excreted in urine after filtration and processing.

questions.prompt: Energy metabolism in cellsA mitochondrial preparation consumes 15.0 µmol O₂ while producing 10.5 µmol CO₂. questions.prompt: Energy metabolism in cellsA mitochondrial preparation consumes 15.0 µmol O₂ while producing 10.5 µmol CO₂. scheme: 1 · Light excites electrons in photosynthetic reaction centres.

questions.prompt: Managing a fragmented speciesA mammal survives in three small isolated woodland populations. Managers propose habitat corridors, captive breeding and later reintroduction. questions.prompt: Flooding, drought and carbon gainTwo woodland areas alternate between waterlogging and dry conditions. In a chamber, illuminated shoots show net oxygen production of 8.0 cm³ h⁻¹; in darkness, equal tissue consumes 2.0 cm³ O₂ h⁻¹. Assume for calculation that respiration in light equals respiration in darkness. During drought, stomatal aperture decreases. Explain how stomatal closure affects water loss and can restrict carbon gain.
scheme: 1 · Closure increases resistance to water-vapour diffusion and reduces transpiration.
2 · It reduces evaporative demand driving xylem tension.
3 · It also restricts carbon dioxide entry.
4 · Reduced carbon supply can limit carbon fixation and carbohydrate production.

questions.prompt: Flooding, drought and carbon gainTwo woodland areas alternate between waterlogging and dry conditions. In a chamber, illuminated shoots show net oxygen production of 8.0 cm³ h⁻¹; in darkness, equal tissue consumes 2.0 cm³ O₂ h⁻¹. Assume for calculation that respiration in light equals respiration in darkness. During drought, stomatal aperture decreases. Explain how waterlogging may alter nitrogen supply and community composition.
scheme: 1 · Low oxygen can limit aerobic root and microbial processes.
2 · Suitable low-oxygen conditions can favour denitrification.
3 · Conversion of nitrate to nitrogen gas reduces available nitrate.
4 · Species differ in tolerance and resource use, changing relative survival or growth.

questions.prompt: Producing an antigen for a vaccineA laboratory identifies a viral surface-protein coding sequence and expresses an appropriate version in a host-cell system. The purified protein is investigated as a vaccine antigen. A later viral population has an altered surface-protein sequence. Explain how vaccination can produce a faster response after later exposure.
scheme: 1 · Specific lymphocytes recognise antigen and are activated.
2 · Clonal expansion produces effector cells.
3 · Memory lymphocytes persist.
4 · Re-exposure generates a faster and larger antigen-specific response.

questions.prompt: Producing an antigen for a vaccineA laboratory identifies a viral surface-protein coding sequence and expresses an appropriate version in a host-cell system. The purified protein is investigated as a vaccine antigen. A later viral population has an altered surface-protein sequence. Explain three requirements for PCR amplification.
scheme: 1 · Primers anneal to sequences flanking the target.
2 · A thermostable DNA polymerase extends primers.
3 · Thermal cycling separates strands, permits annealing and supports extension with free nucleotides.

questions.prompt: Producing an antigen for a vaccineA laboratory identifies a viral surface-protein coding sequence and expresses an appropriate version in a host-cell system. The purified protein is investigated as a vaccine antigen. A later viral population has an altered surface-protein sequence. Explain four issues in expressing and purifying a functional antigen.
scheme: 1 · The coding sequence and regulatory features must suit the host.
2 · The protein must fold appropriately and receive necessary modifications.
3 · Successful constructs must be selected or screened and expression verified.
4 · Quality checks must assess identity, contamination and retained antigenic function.

questions.prompt: Producing an antigen for a vaccineA laboratory identifies a viral surface-protein coding sequence and expresses an appropriate version in a host-cell system. The purified protein is investigated as a vaccine antigen. A later viral population has an altered surface-protein sequence. Explain how immune selection can increase a variant with altered antibody recognition.
scheme: 1 · Mutation supplies heritable sequence variation.
2 · Less effectively recognised variants may reproduce or transmit more successfully.
3 · Their frequency can increase without mutations being directed by the need for immune evasion.

questions.prompt: An inhibitor affects an active animalA compound inhibits the terminal mitochondrial electron-transfer step without directly blocking ion channels or myosin. Researchers investigate a repeatedly stimulated skeletal muscle and the systems supplying it. Explain why the inhibitor reduces oxidative ATP synthesis.
scheme: 1 · Oxygen cannot accept electrons normally at the terminal step.
2 · Carriers remain reduced and normal electron flow is restricted.
3 · Electron-transport-linked proton pumping declines.
4 · The proton gradient is not adequately maintained.
5 · ATP synthase has less proton-motive driving force.

questions.prompt: An inhibitor affects an active animalA compound inhibits the terminal mitochondrial electron-transfer step without directly blocking ion channels or myosin. Researchers investigate a repeatedly stimulated skeletal muscle and the systems supplying it. Explain why prolonged ATP shortage impairs neuronal signalling despite unblocked channels.
scheme: 1 · The sodium–potassium pump requires ATP.
2 · Reduced pumping allows sodium and potassium gradients to deteriorate.
3 · Resting potential and the driving forces for ionic currents are affected.
4 · Reliable impulse generation and recovery can fail.

questions.prompt: An inhibitor affects an active animalA compound inhibits the terminal mitochondrial electron-transfer step without directly blocking ion channels or myosin. Researchers investigate a repeatedly stimulated skeletal muscle and the systems supplying it. Explain ATP requirements in muscle and why glycolysis may temporarily continue.
scheme: 1 · ATP binding enables myosin detachment and further cycling.
2 · ATP supports calcium pumping during relaxation.
3 · Reduction of pyruvate to lactate regenerates NAD.
4 · Glycolysis can then make a small ATP supply by substrate-level phosphorylation, insufficient for sustained normal high output.

questions.prompt: An inhibitor affects an active animalA compound inhibits the terminal mitochondrial electron-transfer step without directly blocking ion channels or myosin. Researchers investigate a repeatedly stimulated skeletal muscle and the systems supplying it. Explain why increased cardiac output cannot fully overcome the inhibitor.
scheme: 1 · Higher output can increase oxygen delivery.
2 · The inhibited terminal pathway cannot use that oxygen normally.
3 · The limitation is cellular utilisation, so supply alone does not restore oxidative phosphorylation.

questions.prompt: A threatened butterfly populationInvestigators mark and release 40 butterflies. After mixing, they capture 50, including 10 marked individuals. A separate large reference population has a recessive phenotype frequency of 0.04. The threatened population becomes fragmented into small isolated groups. Estimate population size and state three assumptions.
scheme: 1 · Population estimate = 40 × 50 / 10 = 200.
2 · Marks remain identifiable without altering survival or capture probability.
3 · Marked individuals mix randomly.
4 · The population is sufficiently closed over the interval.

questions.prompt: A threatened butterfly populationInvestigators mark and release 40 butterflies. After mixing, they capture 50, including 10 marked individuals. A separate large reference population has a recessive phenotype frequency of 0.04. The threatened population becomes fragmented into small isolated groups. Calculate reference-population heterozygote frequency under Hardy–Weinberg.

A threatened butterfly populationInvestigators mark and release 40 butterflies. After mixing, they capture 50, including 10 marked individuals. A separate large reference population has a recessive phenotype frequency of 0.04. The threatened population becomes fragmented into small isolated groups. Explain fragmentation effects on diversity and evaluate one management response.
scheme: 1 · Small groups undergo stronger chance changes through drift.
2 · Isolation reduces gene flow.
3 · Inbreeding increases homozygosity and can expose harmful recessive alleles.
4 · Corridors or carefully managed movement can support gene flow.
5 · Monitor habitat, disease and genetic outcomes rather than assuming movement is always beneficial.
